question: What should the landing page lead with?
notes: Same content, same palette, same type scale, same build — captured at the same 1200px viewport. Only the order of the argument differs: one states the promise and then proves it, the other shows the proof first and explains it after.
how: Read only the top third, the way someone who has never heard of this reads it. One of these asks you to take a claim on faith for four lines. The other shows you a machine refusing an agent before it says a word about why. Then check the live pages and narrow the window — one of them holds up at phone width and one does not.

map.A: proof first — the actual deny message is the hero, the headline explains what you just read
map.B: promise first — headline states the claim, the refusal appears lower as evidence

blocks.text:
Leads with the one thing no competitor can show: an agent being refused mid-write. It is concrete, it is unfamiliar, and it cannot be written by a tool that does not do it.

The cost: it demands ten seconds of reading a terminal message before any context, and a reader who does not already know what a coding agent is will bounce off it entirely.

Conventional and legible. A stranger reads a claim they can evaluate in one breath, and the proof is waiting below when they want it.

The cost: 'your agents ask once, your answer stands' is a sentence any tool could write. Nothing in the first screen is falsifiable, and the thing that makes stet unlike anything else is below the fold.
